# Facet normals overestimate the global depth of complete-lattice simplex families
OC to facet-parallel continuous normals. It treats actual convex bodies,
complete lattice bases, a nonaffine concave common-vertex radius, and
every number of integer variables. It is not a counterexample to OC.

## 1. The family and the precise statement

Let T={(x1,x2):x1,x2>=0, x1+x2<=1}, with area V=1/2.
For every integer n>=1 put

    B_n=[-1,1] times [0,1]^(n-1),
    r(z)=1-|z1|/2,
    C_n={(z,x):z in B_n, x in r(z)T}.

This is a full-dimensional compact convex body: besides the box and
x_i>=0 constraints it has the two affine inequalities

    x1+x2+z1/2<=1,   x1+x2-z1/2<=1.

Its complete integer base is

    P_n={-1,0,1} times {0,1}^(n-1),

and all its fibers have positive area. Its intrinsic dimension q is
therefore 2 and its measure is the sum of fiber areas. The radius is
concave and genuinely nonaffine.

Call an ambient halfspace a facet-restricted cap if its continuous
normal is parallel to one of the three facet normals of T, with
either orientation. Include purely integer-normal halfspaces as well.
Integer coefficients and thresholds are completely unrestricted in
this definition. Thus the six continuous directions are

    +/-e1, +/-e2, +/-(1,1).

Let depth_F be depth using just this restricted family and depth be
ordinary depth using every closed ambient halfspace. Set

    t=(sqrt(21)-4)/2,
    U=4t^2+1/4=(149-32sqrt(21))/4,
    epsilon=1/2000.

Then

    max_(y in S_n) depth_F(y)
       =(149-32sqrt(21))/(6*2^(n-1)),                         (1)

whereas

    max_(y in S_n) depth(y)
       <=(149-32sqrt(21))/(6*2^(n-1))
                              -1/(3000*2^(n-1)).             (2)

In particular facet directions do not determine the GLOBAL maximum
depth, even after optimizing the point in S and every integer tilt.
The normalized gap is explicit and strictly positive for every n.

For the three-fiber case n=1, at the unique facet-restricted maximizing
point, the full cap-mass function also has a nonfacet stationary local
minimum with positive-definite Hessian in its continuous-angle and
integer-tilt parameters. This is proved in Section 5.

Affine translations of the fibers can be added by any map
(z,x)->(z,x+A z+b). This is an invertible affine shear preserving
integer bases, all halfspaces, and each fiber's area. A common
invertible continuous linear map likewise replaces T by any fixed
triangle and multiplies every area by the same determinant. No
nonaffine recentering of r(z)T is used: its centroid r(z)(1/3,1/3)
is itself a nonaffine function of the base.

## 2. An exact two-cap identity

For r>0 and h real,

    inf_(p+q=2h)
       [clamp(p,0,r)^2+clamp(q,0,r)^2]
       =min{r^2,2(h_+)^2}.                              (3)

If one term is saturated at r^2, the sum is at least r^2.
Otherwise the sum is p_+^2+q_+^2, at least 2(h_+)^2 by convexity.
For the converse, one can make one term full and the other empty;
when 2(h_+)^2<=r^2, the choice p=q=h attains the other value
(with the obvious zero case h<=0). Thus (3) is an attained infimum,
not merely a lower bound.

We first work at n=1. The fiber radii at bases -1,0,1 are
1/2,1,1/2, so total mass is (3/2)V. Every following raw cap value is
divided by V.

A middle candidate has coordinates (0,x1,x2), x_i>=0 and x1+x2<=1.
For the direction x_i>=x_i(candidate), minimizing over every integer
tilt gives exactly

    A(x_i)=(1-x_i)^2+min{1/4,2(1/2-x_i)_+^2}.          (4)

Indeed the central tail is (1-x_i)^2, and the two endpoint cap
lengths have sum 1-2x_i; their clipped squared lengths are governed
by (3). The function A is strictly decreasing on [0,1].

For the direction x1+x2<=s, s=x1(candidate)+x2(candidate), the central
mass is s^2. The endpoint thresholds have sum 2s, so (3) gives

    B(s)=s^2+min{1/4,2s^2}.                           (5)

This function is strictly increasing on [0,1]. Both formulas include
all real base tilts, saturation, and closed boundaries.

## 3. The exact global facet-restricted maximum

The number t is the positive root of

    t^2+4t-5/4=0,

and satisfies

    233/800 < t < 583/2000,
    29/100 < t < 3/10.                                (6)

These are exact bounds obtained by squaring the positive rational
bounds on sqrt(21). They imply that the branches in (4)--(5) at
(t,2t) are

    A(t)=(1-t)^2+2(1/2-t)^2,
    B(2t)=4t^2+1/4.

The quadratic equation says precisely that A(t)=B(2t)=U.

At any middle candidate, its restricted depth is at most
min{A(x1),A(x2),B(x1+x2)}V. If that minimum is at least U V,
strict monotonicity forces x1<=t, x2<=t, and x1+x2>=2t.
Hence x1=x2=t. This proves the universal upper bound U V and
uniqueness of a possible middle maximizing point.

All the other permitted cap orientations have mass at least U V
through this point. For x_i<=t, the own contribution is 2t-t^2.
The endpoint infimum is 1/4 because their thresholds have sum 2t>1/2.
For completeness, if neither endpoint is full, their thresholds
q1,q2 lie in [0,r], r=1/2, and

    sum (2r q_i-q_i^2)>=r(q1+q2)>r^2;

if one threshold is negative the other exceeds r and is full.
A full/empty pair attains r^2. Thus the exact negative-coordinate
minimum is

    2t-t^2+1/4 > U,

the difference being t(2-5t)>0.

For x1+x2>=2t, both endpoints can be empty simultaneously, since
2t>1/2. The exact minimum is the middle mass 1-4t^2, and

    1-4t^2-U=3/4-8t^2>0

by t<3/10. Purely integer caps through the middle base have mass at
least 5V/4, also greater than U V. These arguments exhaust both
orientations of every facet normal. A containing cap may first be
translated to pass through the candidate, which cannot increase
its mass. Consequently the restricted depth at (0,t,t) is exactly U V.

At an endpoint base, the three own triangle centroid facet caps
cover the entire fiber and each has raw mass (4/9)(1/4)V=V/9 after
isolating that fiber by a finite base tilt. Thus no endpoint can
compete with U V. Explicitly, for the left endpoint the two caps

    x_i-(z+1)>=1/6

and the cap

    -x1-x2-(z+1)>=-1/3

isolate that endpoint and cover its fiber. For the right endpoint
replace -(z+1) by +(z-1). The other two fibers are strictly excluded.
This proves (1) when n=1.

## 4. A finite nonfacet cover strictly improves the global upper bound

Fix a=9/10 and define

    t1=t-(17/10)epsilon,
    t2=t+epsilon,
    s=2t-epsilon.

Consider these three ambient caps:

    H1: a x1+(1-a)x2 >= t1,
    H2: x2 >= t2,
    H3: -x1-x2+s z >= -s.                            (7)

Their restrictions to the entire middle plane form a closed cover.
In fact the positive weights 1, 2a-1=4/5, a=9/10 cancel the
continuous normals, and their weighted threshold is zero because

    t1+(2a-1)t2-a s=0.                                (8)

If all three margins were negative, their weighted sum would be
negative rather than zero. This proves the cover for every middle
point, without selecting a center or relying on a limiting argument.

For a radius-r triangle and a in (1/2,1), the one-vertex cap
a x1+(1-a)x2>=q has relative area

    (ar-q)^2/[a(2a-1)]

whenever (1-a)r<q<ar. These inequalities hold strictly for all
three fibers of H1, by (6). The cap values in (7), divided by V, are

    F1=[(a-t1)^2+2(a/2-t1)^2]/[a(2a-1)],
    F2=(1-t2)^2+2(1/2-t2)^2,
    F3=s^2+1/4.                                      (9)

For H3, the left endpoint threshold is zero and its area is zero,
while the right threshold 2s exceeds 1/2 and captures that whole
endpoint. The central threshold s is strictly between zero and one.

Each expression in (9) is strictly less than U-epsilon. Here are
explicit rational estimates establishing the gap.

For the unshifted first cap, exact substitution using
t^2+4t=5/4 gives

    U-[(a-t)^2+2(a/2-t)^2]/[a(2a-1)]
       =(136sqrt(21)-623)/48 > 11/2400.                (10)

The last strict inequality uses sqrt(21)>1833/400; squaring gives
21*400^2-1833^2=111>0. On the interval [t1,t], the magnitude of the
derivative of the first cap value with respect to its threshold q is

    (4a-6q)/[a(2a-1)]<3.

Indeed q>1/4, q<3/10, and the denominator is 18/25.
Lowering the threshold by (17/10)epsilon therefore increases the
mass by less than 51/20000. The remaining deficit is greater than

    11/2400-51/20000=61/30000>epsilon.

For the second cap, exact expansion yields

    U-F2=epsilon(4-6t)-3epsilon^2>epsilon

using t<3/10. For the third,

    U-F3=4t epsilon-epsilon^2>epsilon

using t>29/100. All branch conditions and inequalities are checked
also by the accompanying exact quadratic-field verifier.

The three caps cover every middle candidate and each has mass
less than (U-epsilon)V. The six endpoint-isolating caps in Section 3
cover both endpoint fibers and have mass V/9<(U-epsilon)V.
We have therefore exhibited a finite ambient halfspace cover of S
whose every member has mass at most (U-epsilon)V. Every possible
center lies in one member of that cover. Hence

    max depth <=(2/3)(U-epsilon)

at n=1, proving the explicit strict improvement. This proof uses
actual fixed closed caps; no continuity or merely pointwise gap is
being promoted to a global gap.

## 5. A genuine nonfacet stationary cap with positive Hessian

At the restricted maximizing point y0=(0,t,t), consider the full
two-parameter chart of through-point cap directions

    a x1+(1-a)x2+beta z >= t.                         (11)

Near a in [17/20,9/10] and beta=0, all three traces are proper
one-vertex cuts, because (1-a)r<t<ar for r=1/2 and r=1.
Their total mass divided by V is exactly

    F(a,beta)
      =[(a-t)^2+2(a/2-t)^2+2beta^2]/[a(2a-1)].       (12)

In particular F_beta(a,0)=0 and the mixed derivative F_a,beta(a,0)
vanishes. The a-derivative at beta=0 is

    F_a(a,0)=Q(a)/[a(2a-1)]^2,
    Q(a)=(8t-3/2)a^2-12t^2 a+3t^2.                 (13)

Using the exact interval (6), one obtains

    Q(17/20)<0<Q(9/10).

For example, eliminating t^2 gives
Q(17/20)=(1729/50)t-8067/800 and
Q(9/10)=(942/25)t-2193/200, whose signs follow from (6).
Furthermore Q' is positive throughout this interval. A simple lower
bound, using t>29/100 and t<3/10, is

    Q'(a)
      >2(41/50)(17/20)-12(3/10)^2>0.

There is therefore a unique root a* in (17/20,9/10). At (a*,0),

    F_aa=Q'(a*)/[a*(2a*-1)]^2>0,
    F_beta,beta=4/[a*(2a*-1)]>0,
    F_a,beta=0.                                      (14)

Thus the Hessian is positive definite and this cap is a strict local
minimum in the complete local space of oriented through-point
halfspaces. Positive rescaling has been removed by the normalization
u1+u2=1; (a,beta) are genuine coordinates on that open chart.

Its continuous normal (a*,1-a*) is parallel to no facet normal of T.
The stationarity comes from a sum of three different slice responses,
not from making each individual simplex cap stationary. Consequently
an ordinary one-simplex Hessian test cannot be applied separately to
each fiber and then summed. In particular the archived theorem that
excludes stationary caps containing at least two positive vertices in
one simplex does not apply: each of the three cuts here includes
exactly one simplex vertex. The endpoint planes are not required to
pass through interior points of their own fibers.

## 6. Every integer dimension and exact affine scope

For n>1, fix a vertex b of {0,1}^(n-1). Its three-fiber copy is a
literal copy of the n=1 source. Any ambient cap through a point of
this copy restricts either to a genuine cap of the copy or to the
entire copy. The latter possibility occurs when its restricted normal
vanishes; its raw mass is then the full copy mass. In either case the
raw mass is at least the copy's corresponding depth. Conversely every cap of the copy can
be extended to the full family while excluding all other copies:
add a sufficiently large multiple of an affine function of the other
integer coordinates which is zero at b and strictly negative at all
other cube vertices. Boundedness of the continuous fibers makes a
finite coefficient sufficient. This operation keeps the continuous
normal fixed, so it applies equally to unrestricted and facet-restricted
caps.

The full raw point depth is thus exactly the raw point depth in its
own three-fiber copy, in both cap families. There are 2^(n-1) equal
copies and total mass (3/2)V*2^(n-1). Dividing the results of Sections
3--4 proves (1)--(2) for every n>=1. Equivalently, extend the explicit
finite covers copy by copy with those finite isolating coefficients.

The bodies have a complete lattice base throughout this construction.
The product in the additional integer directions does not change the
nonaffine roof in z1, and no nonlinear centroid translation is used.
Common continuous affine images and affine translation shears retain
the strict gap with the same normalized constants.

## 7. The example is OC-safe

At the centroid of any middle radius-one fiber, its own ordinary
Grunbaum contribution is (4/9)V for every containing ambient cap.
Thus this point has normalized depth at least

    (8/27)/2^(n-1)=16/(27*2^n)>4/(9*2^n).

The right side is the required OC constant for d=2. Purely integer
normals contain the full own fiber and satisfy the same lower bound.
The example only rules out computing the sharp mixed depth by facet
directions; it does not challenge OC.

The exact standard-library verifier is

    work/verify_global_simplex_facet_restriction_obstruction.py.

It verifies the quadratic-field identities, all cap regimes, all
six oriented facet comparisons, the finite cover, its explicit gap,
and the stationary Hessian signs. Its arithmetic is entirely rational
in the real field Q(sqrt(21)); no numerical optimizer is a premise.
